  "brief_title": "Hurst Exponent Analysis of LOB Volume Profiles in Futures Markets",
  "domain_id": "quant_research_scout",
  "executive_summary": "This brief synthesizes empirical evidence regarding the Hurst exponent (long memory) for limit order book (LOB) volume profiles across various futures assets. Analysis of mean Hurst exponents across different sub-sampled time increments (from 1 second to 1 minute) reveals significant long-range dependence in volume profiles, with values consistently above 0.5. The data shows that as the time increment increases, the Hurst exponent generally decreases, though it remains indicative of persistent behavior across all observed assets and time scales.",
  "formal_expression_or_rule": "H > 0.5 indicates long-range dependence (persistence) in the LOB volume profiles.",
  "core_findings_and_rules": [
    "All observed assets (5YTN, BOBL, SP500, NIKKEI, GOLD, SILVER) exhibit Hurst exponents greater than 0.5, indicating long-range dependence in LOB volume profiles.",
    "The Hurst exponent is highest at the 1-second sampling frequency and decreases as the sampling interval increases to 1 minute.",
    "NIKKEI exhibits the highest levels of persistence (Hurst exponent), reaching up to 0.9020 at the 1-second interval.",
    "The magnitude of the Hurst exponent is generally higher for the 'Ask' side compared to the 'Bid' side in certain assets like BOBL and SP500, though they are often closely matched.",
    "The relationship between time scale and Hurst exponent is inverse: higher frequency (shorter time increments) results in higher Hurst exponents."
  ],
  "domain_constraints_and_caveats": [
    "The data represents mean Hurst exponents across all trading days using varying sub-sampled data for level 1 of the LOB.",
    "The results are specific to the provided asset classes and the 1-second to 1-minute sampling window."
  ],
  "known_risks_and_failure_modes": [
    "As the time increment increases (e.g., moving from 1 second to 1 minute), the Hurst exponent decreases, suggesting that the strength of the perceived long-range dependence weakens at coarser time scales."
  ],
